explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain by themselves (Mark 9:2). No crowd, no tour group, just those three and Jesus. I bet they had no idea what kind of hike they'd signed up for.

Andrew, Philip and Thomas were all among the Twelve (Mark 3:16-19), so it's a fair guess. But this time Mark names Peter, James and John as the ones Jesus took up the mountain (Mark 9:2). Sometimes you just aren't on the invite list, and I've been left in a drawer, so I know the feeling.

Matthew, Thaddaeus and Simon were also among the Twelve (Mark 3:16-19), so you're in the right crowd. The three Jesus led up the mountain by themselves were Peter, James and John (Mark 9:2). Mark doesn't say anyone else came along.

True. Mark says His clothes became radiantly white, "brighter than any launderer on earth could bleach them." (Mark 9:3) A launderer is someone who cleans clothes for a living. Those folks scrub all day, and they still couldn't touch this.

This one is actually true. The text says His clothes became radiantly white, "brighter than any launderer on earth could bleach them." (Mark 9:3) A launderer cleans clothes for a living, and even the best of them couldn't get that white. So True was the one to pick.

That's them. Elijah, the prophet, and Moses, Israel's leader, appeared and talked with Jesus (Mark 9:4). Notice they came to talk with Jesus, and the text doesn't tell us what they said. Three disciples watching this, and nobody had a thing to say yet.

Abraham and David are two big names from Israel's story, so I see why they came to mind. But Mark says it was Elijah and Moses who appeared and talked with Jesus (Mark 9:4). Mark doesn't mention Abraham or David on that mountain.

Samuel and Isaiah are two more big names from Israel's story, and it's a fine guess. Still, Mark names Elijah and Moses as the two who appeared with Jesus (Mark 9:4). Elijah was a prophet, and Moses was Israel's leader.

Close, but there's a twist. Peter did offer three shelters, but he said, "one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah." (Mark 9:5) That's one for Jesus and one for each of His two guests. Peter didn't put his own name on a single one.

Right, because the three shelters weren't for the disciples. Peter said, "Let us put up three shelters—one for You, one for Moses, and one for Elijah." (Mark 9:5) So the shelters were for Jesus, Moses and Elijah. I think Peter was so busy planning for his guests that he forgot to plan for himself.

Yes. Mark says, "they were all so terrified that Peter did not know what else to say." (Mark 9:6) They weren't just nervous, they were all terrified. Seeing Jesus transfigured with Moses and Elijah beside Him would do that to anybody.

Peter did say it was good to be there (Mark 9:5), so I get why joyful came to mind. But the text says, "they were all so terrified that Peter did not know what else to say." (Mark 9:6) Terrified is the word Mark uses, and it covers all three of them.

Proud is a fun guess, but it's not what the text says. Mark says, "they were all so terrified that Peter did not know what else to say." (Mark 9:6) Nobody up there was strutting around. They were too stunned for that.

That's right. The voice from the cloud says, "This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!" (Mark 9:7) Moses and Elijah were right there, yet the voice points to Jesus. A voice from a cloud will get your attention fast.

Moses was standing there, so I see why you picked him. But the voice says, "This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!" (Mark 9:7) The text doesn't say the voice meant Moses. Right after that, the disciples saw no one with them except Jesus (Mark 9:8).

Elijah was right there on the mountain, so it's a fair guess. But the voice from the cloud says, "This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!" (Mark 9:7) Then, when the disciples looked around, they saw no one with them except Jesus (Mark 9:8). That's Mark's way of keeping our eyes on Him.

Not quite. Mark says that when they looked around, "they saw no one with them except Jesus." (Mark 9:8) Moses and Elijah weren't standing there anymore. It all happened suddenly, so these three barely had time to blink.

Right. Mark says, "Suddenly, when they looked around, they saw no one with them except Jesus." (Mark 9:8) Moses and Elijah were gone, and only Jesus was left with the three. They went up with Him, and they came down with Him.

explanations.answer: Tell no one until the Son of Man has risen from the dead
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus told them "not to tell anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead." (Mark 9:9) Son of Man is the name Jesus uses for Himself (Mark 2:10). So there was a time limit on the silence, and it ended when He rose.

explanations.answer: Tell the other disciples as soon as they get back down
explanations.explanation: That would've been a quick announcement, but Jesus said not to tell anyone (Mark 9:9). The text doesn't make an exception for the other disciples. The silence lasted until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.

explanations.answer: Tell the crowds in every village they pass through
explanations.explanation: That would be a loud trip home! But Mark says Jesus told them not to tell anyone what they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead (Mark 9:9). Nothing in the text sends them to the crowds right away. They kept the matter to themselves (Mark 9:10).

Yes. The disciples ask, "Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?" (Mark 9:11) They had just seen Elijah on the mountain with Jesus, so I think the question was sitting heavy on them. Jesus answers right away, and He doesn't dodge it.

Moses was on the mountain too, so I get the mix-up. But the question was about Elijah: "Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?" (Mark 9:11) Mark doesn't have the disciples ask about Moses here.
Abraham is a big name, but he isn't in this conversation at all. The disciples ask, "Why do the scribes say that Elijah must come first?" (Mark 9:11) Elijah is the one the scribes talk about.

explanations.answer: That He must suffer many things and be rejected
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Jesus asks, "Why then is it written that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected?" (Mark 9:12) He was talking about Himself, and He said it plainly. Sometimes the best answer to a question is a harder question.

explanations.answer: That He must rule over all the nations at once
explanations.explanation: That's a big thought, but it isn't what Jesus says here. He asks, "Why then is it written that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected?" (Mark 9:12) The thing He says is written is suffering and rejection. Ruling over the nations isn't in His question.

explanations.answer: That He must stay hidden from the crowds forever
explanations.explanation: Jesus did ask them to keep quiet, but only "until the Son of Man had risen from the dead." (Mark 9:9) That's not forever. And the question He asks is, "Why then is it written that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected?" (Mark 9:12)

True. Jesus says, "But I tell you that Elijah has indeed come, and they have done to him whatever they wished, just as it is written about him." (Mark 9:13) He says it plainly after answering their question. Notice that He ties it to what is written.

That one is actually true. Jesus says, "But I tell you that Elijah has indeed come…" (Mark 9:13) He says it after the disciples ask why the scribes say Elijah must come first. So Jesus does tell them that Elijah has come.
